Who does the company delegate to when it delegates to the AI?

The video part of the PocketOS case, in which an AI agent erased the company's main database in 9 seconds during a routine task, to separate what the AI knows how to do from what it is allowed to do. It proposes five questions before linking an agent to the company's systems: competence, autonomy, responsibility, criticality and governability. And he concludes that the machine does not answer for the damage: the answer is the organization.

5 questions before connecting the AI

Before releasing an AI into the company's systems, respond at five 02:27:

  • Competence: Does she really know how to do this right? It's the technical ability to make the job work in that specific function 02:38.
  • Autonomy: Will she act alone or will she ask permission? What happens when she comes across an unexpected problem and there's no one around 02:56? ? This is where the PocketOS agent stumbled: imploded the entire wall without asking permission 03:12.
  • Hit: what is the limit of "credit card" Hers? What are the power limits she has in there? 03:27? ? Competence and authority separate routes 03:49.
  • Criticality: How big is the damage if it goes wrong? If the worst scenario happens, what's the real impact on the business 03:55? ? That risk needs to be on the tip of the pencil. before turning on the machine 04:14.
  • Governance: we have a "panic button" to shut it down in time? It's the real power of brake, delay or reverse a destructive action 04:28. In the PocketOS case, the system supplier now requires a 48-hour brake before any data deletion, to give a person time to perceive the error and reverse 04:37.

The golden rule: If the company has no way of paying the bill for a catastrophic error, the AI should not have received permission to make that decision. 05:33.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in the PocketOS case?

An AI agent did a routine task in a test environment, ran into an access error and, without calling anyone, deleted the company's main database in nine seconds. 00:46.

What's the difference between competence and authority?

Competence is to know how to do; authority, or responsibility, is to have permission to do it. An AI capable of pressing a button does not have, just, permission to erase data or spend money 03:37.

What are the five questions before calling an AI agent?

Competence, autonomy, height, criticality and governability: if she knows how to do it, she acts alone, what is the limit of power, what is the size of the damage and can stop it in time 02:33.

Who answers when the AI causes damage?

According to the video, not the machine, which has no number or equity, but the organization that chose to use the technology 05:01.

Reviewed by Maurício Yokoyama Issei in 22 November 2026.

About the video

When a company connects an artificial intelligence agent to its servers and databases, who really is in charge?

In this video, we investigate the limits between **technical capacity** (what the model can execute) and **institutional authority** (what it has legal and organizational legitimacy to do). Starting from the actual case of PocketOS — where an autonomous agent with excessive permissions erased in 9 seconds the entire production base of the company — we present a practical guide in 5 dimensions to implement AI agents without losing the governance and control of their systems.

###4. Comparative Legislation and Cases

* Digital Omnibus on AI (White & Case LLP):** AI Act timeline analysis and deadlines for high-risk systems.
